rationale: The order-topology reference gives the standard order topology, order-convexity and the linear-continuum package. The item consolidates these notions, fixes endpoint and empty-set conventions, and proves the real-line identification inline, so it is a sourced semantic compilation rather than an exact transcription. Source-record correction (Audit-Alpha, wave 3 A6): the UAB topology notes originally recorded alongside it are HTTP 404 and were removed from the item and from this row; Alpha fetched the surviving URL at HTTP 200 and read the cited definitions there.

The sources give separations, connected subsets and the clopen formulation. The item adopts the common convention that the empty space is connected, whereas the Stacks Project explicitly adopts the competing nonempty convention; the item also packages ambient/subspace wording and singleton consequences. The convention delta is explicit and Wikipedia confirms that both conventions occur. Both URLs were retrieved through the model-side web route (HTTP 200).

The source lists the same equivalence between no separation, no nontrivial clopen subset and constancy of maps to the two-point discrete space. The item expands both directions into its dependency-labelled phase format and keeps the empty-space convention explicit; its proof adapts the standard inverse-image argument. The URL was retrieved through the model-side web route (HTTP 200).

The source states that disconnectedness is equivalent to a union of two nonempty separated sets, with separated meaning that neither meets the other's closure. The item recasts this as an ambient-space criterion for a subspace and proves the trace/closure details in library notation. The proof is an adaptation of the standard equivalence. The URL was retrieved through the model-side web route (HTTP 200).

The connected-space reference identifies the connected subsets of the real line with the intervals, that is with the order-convex subsets. The item transports the already-published real-line theorem across the library's identification of the order and metric topologies and includes the empty-set convention, so the statement is a semantic restatement and the short transport proof is local. Source-record correction (Audit-Alpha, wave 3 A6): the UAB topology notes originally recorded alongside it are HTTP 404 and were removed from the item and from this row; Alpha fetched the surviving URL at HTTP 200 and read the cited identification there.

Stacks Lemma 5.7.2 gives the continuous-image theorem with the same hypotheses and conclusion. The item adds the homeomorphism/topological-property corollary and presents the proof through its local clopen characterization; that proof follows the sourced inverse-image argument. The URL was retrieved through the model-side web route (HTTP 200).

The source gives that continuous images of connected spaces are connected and that connected subsets of the real line are intervals. The item composes those results into the topological intermediate-value theorem with explicit endpoint order and equality cases; its proof adapts that standard two-step argument. The URL was retrieved through the model-side web route (HTTP 200).

The sources give the union theorem for a family of connected subsets with common intersection. The item also states the useful hub-set variant in which each member meets one fixed connected set and derives it by adjoining the hub; the proof follows the standard clopen-trace argument. Both URLs were retrieved through the model-side web route (HTTP 200).

Stacks Lemma 5.7.3 states and proves that the closure of a connected set is connected. The item strengthens the packaging to every intermediate set A subset B subset closure(A) and proves it with the same clopen-density mechanism, so the proof is a sourced adaptation rather than a verbatim copy. The URL was retrieved through the model-side web route (HTTP 200).

The sources record preservation of connectedness by products, with the standard finite-support product-topology mechanism. The item supplies an arbitrary-index proof, explicitly separates the empty product, and audits the base-point use of Choice for nonempty factors; that dependency-indexed proof is locally composed. Both URLs were retrieved through the model-side web route (HTTP 200).

The sources give components as maximal connected subsets, quasicomponents as intersections of clopen neighbourhoods, and total disconnectedness via singleton components. The item compiles all three notions and explicitly handles the empty-space and singleton conventions. All URLs were retrieved through the model-side web route (HTTP 200).

Stacks Lemma 5.7.3 gives exactly the partition, uniqueness and closedness properties for components, under its nonempty connected-space convention. The item adds the empty-space boundary and expresses the construction through unions of all connected sets through a point; the proof adapts the sourced union-and-closure proof. The URL was retrieved through the model-side web route (HTTP 200).

Stacks tag 004R states that the component of a point is contained in its quasicomponent and gives the clopen-intersection characterization, and the connected-space reference records the same inclusion with equality under compact Hausdorff or local connectedness. The item also proves that quasicomponents partition the space and are closed unions of components; its proof adapts the standard clopen-complement argument. Source-record correction (Audit-Alpha, wave 3 A6): the Mayer UAB Components notes written here at A4, as the replacement for the unreachable WVU node-9 page, are themselves HTTP 404 and were removed from the item and from this row; Alpha fetched Stacks 004R at HTTP 200 and verified the quasi-component clause in the connected-space reference by reading its source text.

The sources give paths, path-connectedness and path components in the standard unit-interval form. The item packages constant and reversed paths, concatenation and the empty/singleton conventions with local notation, so it is a semantic compilation. Both URLs were retrieved through the model-side web route (HTTP 200).

Bankston's notes give the standard neighbourhood-base definitions of locally connected and locally path-connected spaces. The item states both together, requires the refining neighbourhood itself to be open, and records the equivalent basis language and the vacuous empty-space case. Source-record correction (Audit-Alpha, wave 3 A6): the WVU Math 581 §3.4 page originally recorded alongside it could not be opened by Alpha over https or http and was removed from the item and from this row; Alpha fetched the surviving URL at HTTP 200, and the item also retains the locally-connected-space reference, whose text Alpha read for the same definitions.

Bankston's notes state and prove the iff criterion for local connectedness via components of open subspaces, and the locally-connected-space reference states it verbatim as "A space is locally connected if and only if for every open set U, the connected components of U (in the subspace topology) are open." The item adds the clopen conclusion for components of X and uses the library's explicit ambient/subspace conventions; its proof follows the sourced maximal-component argument. Source-record correction (Audit-Alpha, wave 3 A6): the WVU Math 581 §3.4 page originally recorded alongside them could not be opened by Alpha and was removed from the item and from this row; Alpha fetched both surviving sources at HTTP 200 and read the quoted clause.

The sources state that every path-connected space is connected. The item also locates each path component inside a connected component and treats the empty-space convention; its proof adapts the standard continuous-image-and-common-basepoint union argument. Both URLs were retrieved through the model-side web route (HTTP 200).

Bankston's notes and the locally-connected-space reference state the same theorem and prove it by showing path components are open and then using connectedness. The item makes the component partition and open-complement step explicit in its local phase format; this is a sourced proof adaptation. Source-record correction (Audit-Alpha, wave 3 A6): the WVU Math 581 §3.4 page originally recorded alongside them could not be opened by Alpha and was removed from the item and from this row; Alpha fetched both surviving sources at HTTP 200.

The linear-continuum reference states that the least-upper-bound and order-density conditions are exactly what make an ordered set connected in its order topology, and records that intervals and rays of a linear continuum are connected. The item includes every order-convex subset and supplies the standard supremum-cut proof with explicit endpoint and unbounded cases, so its statement is a semantic restatement and its proof an expanded adaptation. Source-record correction (Audit-Alpha, wave 3 A6): the UAB notes originally recorded here (people.cas.uab.edu/~jcmayer/TopNotes.pdf) are HTTP 404 together with the whole user directory, so they were removed from the item and from this row; Alpha fetched the surviving URL at HTTP 200 and confirmed it carries the cited connectedness content.

MIT's long-line notes and the reference article give the lexicographically ordered omega-one by half-open-unit-interval construction and its order topology. The item distinguishes the closed long ray, open long ray and doubled long line and fixes the endpoint/gluing conventions, so it is a semantic compilation. Both URLs were retrieved through the model-side web route (HTTP 200).

MIT's notes state that the long line is a path-connected linear continuum and use countable ordinal boundedness in its analysis. The item instead proves the closed long ray is a linear continuum and connected, and separately audits the countable-choice dependence of boundedness for at-most-countable subsets; that set-theoretically explicit proof is local. The URL was retrieved through the model-side web route (HTTP 200).

The sources develop the established topologist's-sine-curve pattern: a path-connected oscillating graph whose closure adds a vertical segment and is connected but not path-connected or locally connected. The item replaces sine by an explicitly piecewise-linear zigzag with the same mathematical mechanism, making it a recoverable alteration rather than genuine novelty; its detailed formula, closure computation and no-path proof are locally generated. Both URLs were retrieved through the model-side web route (HTTP 200).

The sources expose the competing empty-space conventions and the standard distinctions among separated sets, connectedness, path-connectedness and local connectedness. The remark is a library-specific compilation of those established conventions and scope choices. Both URLs were retrieved through the model-side web route (HTTP 200).

The sources explicitly document connected spaces that are not path-connected, including the topologist's sine curve and its closure. The item instantiates that standard refutation with the library's piecewise-linear zigzag closure; the short dependency-indexed refutation is local. Both URLs were retrieved through the model-side web route (HTTP 200).

The sources give the closed topologist's sine curve as the closure of an oscillating path-connected graph and state that the closure is not path-connected. The item uses the piecewise-linear zigzag analogue and delegates the computation to its local lemma, so the refutation text is locally generated. Both URLs were retrieved through the model-side web route (HTTP 200).

The sources identify the topologist's sine curve as connected but not locally connected. The item transfers the same obstruction to the library's polygonal zigzag closure and relies on the locally proved witness, so the exact refutation is local while the mathematical phenomenon is established. Both URLs were retrieved through the model-side web route (HTTP 200).

The source expressly notes that intersections of connected sets need not be connected. The item supplies a concrete unit-square-boundary witness with nonempty intersection and verifies both three-sided sets by standard union arguments; that witness proof is local. The URL was retrieved through the model-side web route (HTTP 200).

The sources state that the rational line has singleton components which are not open, giving the standard counterexample to total disconnectedness implying discreteness. The item expands the density and subspace arguments in library notation; that refutation is local. Both URLs were retrieved through the model-side web route (HTTP 200).

The sources record that convex subsets of Euclidean space are connected/path-connected and use the line-segment path. The item includes norm balls for the one-, two- and infinity-norm metrics and expands the triangle-inequality computation; that proof adapts the standard straight-line argument. The current item, however, omits the dependency that establishes the displayed p-norm functions are norms; this is reported separately as a citation-precision proposal and does not make the mathematical statement false. Both URLs were retrieved through the model-side web route (HTTP 200).

The sources give the connectedness or stronger hyper/ultraconnectedness properties of the particular-point, excluded-point, cocountable and cofinite examples; the discrete and indiscrete boundary cases are standard consequences of the definitions. The item compiles six topologies into one hierarchy and proves each row directly, so its proof is local. All URLs were retrieved through the model-side web route (HTTP 200).

The sources compute the corresponding component, path-component and local-connectedness behaviour of the topologist's sine curve and related comb examples. This item works out the library's piecewise-linear zigzag variant and cross-checks its exact components and bad locus, so it is a recoverable semantic alteration with a locally generated computation. Both URLs were retrieved through the model-side web route (HTTP 200).

The connected-space source gives the exact irrational-cut proof that distinct rational points lie in different components and notes that the singleton components are not open. The item adds the nowhere-locally-connected conclusion and expands density in the library's copy of Q inside R; its proof adapts the sourced separation. Both URLs were retrieved through the model-side web route (HTTP 200).

The Stacks Project gives a double-limit-point example where a component is strictly smaller than its quasicomponent, and the second source records the same standard phenomenon and ladder mechanism. The item realizes it geometrically with vertical unit segments over 1/(n+1) and proves the exact component and quasicomponent; this is an established counterexample pattern with an expanded proof, not a novel unsourced construction. Both URLs were retrieved through the model-side web route (HTTP 200).

The sources give the long line/ray as a linear continuum with interval-like local structure and discuss its countable boundedness/nonseparability features. The item packages connectedness, local connectedness, convex initial segments and the countable-choice-qualified cofinality claim into one hierarchy; its detailed dependency-indexed derivation is local. Both URLs were retrieved through the model-side web route (HTTP 200).

Conrad's university notes define the deleted comb and its closure, and identify the closure as path-connected but not locally path-connected/locally connected at the limit tooth. The item uses the standard closed comb, specifies every bad point strictly above the base, and expands the neighbourhood-component argument, so its proof is a sourced adaptation. The URL was retrieved through the model-side web route (HTTP 200).

The box-topology reference states that the box topology is neither compact nor connected and carries the standard bounded/unbounded-sequence separation as its worked failure-of-connectedness example. The item expands both openness checks and contrasts the box and product topologies while tracking the factor connectedness, so its proof adapts the sourced argument. Source-record correction (Audit-Alpha, wave 3 A6): the Dartmouth lecture-20 PDF originally recorded alongside it is HTTP 404, together with its directory, and was removed from the item and from this row; Alpha fetched the surviving URL at HTTP 200 and read the quoted clauses in its source text.
